text.p: Northrop Grumman Corp Chairman Kent Kresa said Thursday that Raytheon Corp's $9.5 billion buyout of Hughes Electronics Corp's defense assets changes the defense industry landscape dramatically, but Northrop intends to remain competitive.

"Yes, the landscape has changed and there's another bigger name in the marketplace but that doesn't mean we can't compete sucessfully as we have done in the past," Kresa told Reuters in an interview after the sale was announced.

"It's been difficult (to stay competitive in defense electronics) all along with Lockheed Martin and others. It's a complex area, we've been successful in the past and we're going to continue to be successful," he said.
General Motors Corp agreed to sell the Hughes assets on Thursday to Raytheon in a $9.5 billion deal comprising $5.1 billion in stock and $4.4 billion in debt.
Los Angeles-based Northrop was the other leading bidder in the auction for Hughes, widely regarded as the last major prize in a consolidating defense industry.

The exact amount of Northrop's bid was not announced, but experts said price was only a secondary issue because of the complex nature of the deal, which was structured so that GM could avoid a potentially large capital gains tax bill.
By teaming up with Raytheon, GM is betting the combination of Raytheon and Hughes will fare better in the stock market than a parternship with Northrop.
Kresa said Northrop is prepared to move on.
"If it makes a lot of sense we agressively go for things, but if it doesn't work out we move on," Kresa said. "This would have been a nice fit, but that's life."
"We do the right thing for our shareholders and if something isn't right we won't go that far ... I can't say it's a blow at all," Kresa said.

"We've got the size, capacity and capability to be very sucessful the way we are," he said. "We've said in the past that we see double-digit earnings growth over the next several years and we still believe that's absolutely true."
Kresa said he sees revenues growing to $10 billion with the electronics side of the business accounting for about two thirds of that total by 2000.
"We see ourselves growing from the $8 billion (in revenues) we are today to about $10 billion by the close of the century," he said.
While most analysts are saying the Raytheon/Hughes deal may be the last of the big defense mergers, Kresa said he still thinks nothing can be ruled out.

"There are still some large things around that could go one way or the other. It depends on if people want to stay in the business or not, we'll all learn it as we go forward," he said. "There there could indeed be more integration."

Kresa said he hopes to see employment rise in the next few years as the electronics business grows. On Wednesday, the company announced net job cuts of 755 workers, principally due to the phasing out of the B-2 Stealth bomber project.
Northrop, which had 1995 revenues of $6.8 billion, specializes in electronics and systems integration and commercial and military aircraft aerostructures.

Among its strongest franchises are the Joint Surveillance Target Attack Radar System, known as Joint-STARS, its B-2 Stealth bomber, its production of the fuselage, tail and systems for the F-18 fighter jet, and making fuselage and tail sections of the Boeing 747 and a variety of parts for Boeing Co's 757, 767 and 777 aircraft.
